title: Temptation bundling
hookLine: pairing a treat with a chore, like a favorite audiobook only at the gym, helped people exercise (Milkman and colleagues)

cards: A gripping audiobook, the kind that keeps someone sitting in a parked car to hear the end of a chapter. Now add one rule: it can only be heard at the gym.
The behavioral scientist Katherine Milkman has described trying this on herself. Pair something you crave with something you keep putting off, and let the craving pull you toward the chore.
She gave the idea a name, and then she put it to the test.

teach.b: First, the study. Milkman, Julia Minson and Kevin Volpp offered gym members audiobooks of page-turning novels. In one group, the audiobooks lived on devices kept at the gym, so they could only be heard there.
Those people went to the gym more often than a comparison group, at least at first. Second, the honest fade.
The boost shrank as the weeks went on, especially after a holiday break. Bundling got people moving; it didn't keep running forever on its own.
One way to read that: bundling is a way to get started, while the place, the cue and the reason grow strong enough to carry the habit. Third, how it differs from a prize.
A few days ago, this path saw that an expected reward can turn play into work.
Bundling is built differently: the pleasure isn't a payment handed over afterward. It comes during the activity, as part of it. The chore stops being only a chore.
Fourth, an old word for something close.

Patanjali's Yoga Sutras say that a seated posture should be sthira and sukha: steady, and easy or pleasant. Effort and ease, held together in the same moment. A practice doesn't have to be grim to be serious.
Something pleasant built into it, a cup of tea beside you, a window with a view, a favorite blanket, can be part of what brings you back tomorrow.

how: People who use temptation bundling keep a favorite show, podcast or treat for the moment they do a task they avoid, such as exercise or housework, and only then.

o: pairing a treat you crave with a chore you keep avoiding
giving yourself a prize after finishing a hard task
resisting several temptations at once until they fade

games.q: inside temptation bundling: tap the pairs.

s: the bundling boost lasted unchanged for months
it shrank over the weeks, especially after a holiday break.
people who could only hear the audiobooks at the gym went more, at first
they visited more often than the comparison group early on.
the Yoga Sutras ask for a posture that is only strict and hard
they pair steady with easy: sthira and sukha.

games.q: you've been avoiding folding laundry, and there's one podcast you love. what does temptation bundling suggest?
o: listen whenever you like, and fold when you can.
save the podcast for laundry and nothing else.
promise yourself the podcast after the folding is done.
games.why: bundling puts the pleasure inside the chore, kept for that moment alone, rather than handing it over afterward like a prize.

practice: Before the sit, choose one thing you've been putting off, dishes, a form, a walk, and one small pleasure you'll keep only for it: a playlist, a podcast, the good tea. Hold the pairing in mind for a breath.
Then let it go, and sit, letting the breath be both steady and easy.

wordCard.voice: Temptation bundling. Pairing something you enjoy with something you avoid, so the pleasure comes only with the chore. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit, from Patanjali's Yoga Sutras: ease, pleasantness; a posture should be steady and easy.

carryVoice: Your line: bundle it. Some chores go better with a good story. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Milkman, Minson & Volpp, "Holding the Hunger Games hostage at the gym: An evaluation of temptation bundling"
